name: Baking soda toothpaste
lead: Baking soda toothpaste is a dentifrice that contains sodium bicarbonate, usually alongside fluoride, marketed for plaque removal, stain removal, and neutralising acid and odour. Sodium bicarbonate is classed as a mild abrasive and appears in many "natural" toothpaste formulations [1].

People use it to improve how their teeth and breath look and smell: the abrasive action is meant to lift surface stain from coffee, tea and tobacco so teeth look brighter, while the acid-neutralising and plaque-removal claims relate to fresher breath and healthier-looking gums. The American Dental Association notes that abrasive agents in toothpaste may whiten teeth by physically removing surface stains, whereas peroxides lighten intrinsic stains [8].

Randomised trials in the dental-products field have compared baking soda toothpastes with a regular fluoride toothpaste for plaque and gingivitis and have tested a baking soda formula for tooth sensitivity [2][3][5]. These sources document mostly oral-health outcomes rather than tooth colour.

paras: Abrasives make up roughly 8 to 20 percent of a typical toothpaste and work by physically removing plaque and surface stain. Sodium bicarbonate is listed among the representative abrasives.[1] Abrasivity is commonly expressed as a relative dentin abrasivity (RDA) value; one encyclopedia account says the ANSI and the American Dental Association regard values below 250 as safe for lifetime use.[1]

The ADA states that dentifrices at or below 250 on the relative dentin abrasivity scale are considered safe and effective, that clinical evidence suggests lifelong brushing at or below that level causes limited dentin wear and virtually no enamel wear, and that its Seal of Acceptance for cavity protection requires fluoride [8]. Wikipedia describes sodium bicarbonate as having anticaries and abrasive properties and acting as a mechanical cleanser that neutralises acid in the mouth [9].

sections.h: How it helps teeth look better
paras: People use baking soda toothpaste for a brighter smile and a cleaner mouth. The route to a better look is mechanical: sodium bicarbonate is a mild abrasive that helps lift surface stain from coffee, tea, wine or tobacco, and it is also described as neutralising acid in the mouth.[1][9] Removing surface stain makes teeth look lighter without bleaching, and cleaner gums and less plaque make the whole smile look healthier, which is where the gingivitis trials below come in.[3][5]

A 2017 review in the Journal of the American Dental Association by Yiming Li concluded that baking soda dentifrices are effective and safe for tooth stain removal and thereby for whitening; it reported that several clinical studies found them more effective at stain removal than some non-baking soda dentifrices with higher abrasivity, and that most research used manual rather than powered toothbrushes.[10] The review described baking soda dentifrice as a useful alternative or addition to daily oral hygiene for removing tooth stains.[10]
Sodium bicarbonate was discovered in 1801 by Berlin pharmacist Valentin Rose the Younger, and bakers John Dwight and Austin Church opened the first US factory making baking soda in 1846 [9].

A paste of hydrogen peroxide and baking soda was being recommended for use on toothbrushes by around 1900, and Arm & Hammer sold a baking soda tooth powder in the United States until about 2000.[1] Later patents describe baking soda toothpastes and gels containing soluble pyrophosphate salts.[6][7]

A controlled trial of 208 participants tested a baking soda toothpaste delivering calcium, phosphate and fluoride (Arm and Hammer Enamel Care for Sensitive Teeth, UK) against a control toothpaste for dentinal hypersensitivity over eight weeks. Both groups improved, with mean pain scores in the test group falling by 45.6 percent at week 4 and 61.1 percent at week 8, and the authors reported that the effect persisted for at least eight weeks after switching back to the control [2].

A six-month, double-blind randomised study of 319 participants compared fluoride toothpastes containing 35 percent and 20 percent baking soda with a fluoride control toothpaste, measuring plaque and gingivitis indices at 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months. All three toothpastes reduced the indices versus baseline, and the two baking soda toothpastes reduced them significantly more than the control [3]. At six months the 35 percent and 20 percent baking soda toothpastes had reduced the gingival index, gingival bleeding index and plaque index by 15.0, 46.9 and 18.3 percent and by 9.4, 25.9 and 12.4 percent respectively compared with the control, and the 35 percent product outperformed the 20 percent product on all three measures.[3]

A separate 12-week double-blind trial of 159 participants compared a fluoride toothpaste with 20 percent baking soda with a fluoride control. After 12 weeks, reductions in gingival index, plaque index and gingival bleeding index were 12.6, 9.6 and 44.2 percent respectively versus control, and some benefit remained statistically significant after four weeks of customary hygiene [5].

A 1992 study of 22 dentists examined patient compliance with oral hygiene using a fluoride toothpaste with hydrogen peroxide and baking soda dispensed from a dual package [4]. The stain-removal literature is summarised in the 2017 JADA review rather than in the trials above.[10]
Encyclopedic sources note that abrasive toothpastes cause a small amount of enamel wear and that excessive use of whitening toothpaste might damage enamel.[1]

The ADA says abrasive agents can physically remove surface stain, and its guidance frames abrasivity through the RDA scale instead of a ranking of toothpaste safety [8]. Wikipedia lists the main hazard of pure sodium bicarbonate as eye irritation, with a rat oral LD50 of 4220 mg/kg [9].

Baking soda dentifrices are sold under brands such as Arm and Hammer, and patents from the 1990s describe formulations pairing baking soda with soluble pyrophosphate salts for tartar control [6][7]. A paste of hydrogen peroxide and baking soda was already recommended for toothbrushes by around 1900, and Arm and Hammer sold a tooth powder in the US until about 2000 [1]. Baking soda is also a common ingredient in home-made whitening and natural-toothpaste routines, where it is combined with other household items.

In home routines, baking soda is used alone or with hydrogen peroxide as a do-it-yourself whitening approach. A 2008 T Nation thread on teeth whitening describes sprinkling baking soda on a toothbrush after hydrogen peroxide and says a dentist had recommended it, while a 2004 thread poster said they would rather not brush with that combination regularly, and a 2023 poster said they use baking soda instead of toothpaste because it is milder.[11][12][13] The American Dental Association's guidance frames abrasivity through the relative dentin abrasivity scale, with values at or below 250 considered safe and effective, and says its cavity-protection Seal requires fluoride.[8]

timeline.event: A hydrogen peroxide and baking soda paste is recommended for toothbrush use.[1]

card.summary: Sodium bicarbonate toothpaste sold for plaque, stain and odour control; the research is mostly on gum health, not whitening.
card.note: Abrasive; whitening effects are not established in the studies reviewed.

quick.overview:
Baking soda toothpaste is an ordinary fluoride toothpaste that includes sodium bicarbonate, a mild abrasive. It is sold for plaque removal, surface stain removal and neutralising acid and odour.

Published trials mostly look at plaque, gum inflammation and tooth sensitivity rather than visible whitening, so its appearance benefit rests largely on the general role of abrasives in removing surface stain.
quick.mechanism: Sodium bicarbonate acts as a mild abrasive that helps lift plaque and surface stain mechanically while brushing; manufacturers also describe it as neutralising acids and odours.
quick.risks: Abrasive toothpastes cause a small amount of enamel wear, and excessive use of whitening pastes might damage enamel according to encyclopedic sources. Abrasivity is rated by RDA value, with values under 250 considered acceptable by ANSI and the ADA.

chain: Sodium bicarbonate acts as a mild abrasive while brushing
Surface stain and plaque are lifted from the enamel
Teeth look brighter, breath fresher and gums less inflamed
angle.text: Baking soda toothpaste is a brushing product: the abrasive removes surface stain and plaque, which people associate with brighter-looking teeth and fresher breath. The studies on it measure plaque, gum inflammation and sensitivity.
